title: Vikings beat him there by 471 years.
description:
Vikings beat him there by 471 years. Not legend, a dated find: European wood, cut with metal tools nobody in the area had, at the northern tip of Newfoundland.

Nobody could say exactly when it was occupied for another 61 years. Archaeologist Anne Stine Ingstad excavated it through the 1960s and dated it to "around 1000 AD" by comparing it with sites in Greenland and Iceland, a good estimate, not a year.

A cosmic-ray spike from the year 993 is baked into tree rings everywhere on Earth. Researchers counted growth rings outward from that marked ring, on wood the Norse had felled and shaped, straight to the year they cut it.

The exact year, from 127 radiocarbon measurements across four wooden objects. Not "around 1000". Not a century. One year.

Led the University of Groningen team that published the date in Nature, using the 993 solar storm as a fixed marker buried in the rings of every sample tested.

Sources:
- https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-021-03972-8: Kuitems, M., Wallace, B.L., Lindsay, C. et al., "Evidence for European presence in the Americas in AD 1021," Nature (2021), read via abstract and multiple direct quotations in secondary science reporting (below). Establishes the AD 1021 date for Norse-cut wood at L'Anse aux Meadows.
- https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/new-dating-method-shows-vikings-occupied-newfoundland-in-1021-ce-180978903/: Smithsonian Magazine, read directly. Establishes the method: a cosmic-ray-driven radiocarbon spike from a known solar storm in AD 993 is preserved in tree rings worldwide; researchers counted growth rings out from that marker ring to the bark edge on wood cut with metal blades, tools the region's Indigenous population did not have, landing on AD 1021.
- https://www.sciencenews.org/article/vikings-north-america-date-newfoundland: Science News, read directly. Establishes the numbers: 127 radiocarbon measurements across 83 tree rings from four wooden objects, three of which retained their outermost growth ring; calls it the oldest precise date for Europeans in the Americas and the only one predating Columbus's 1492 voyage.
- https://parks.canada.ca/lhn-nhs/nl/meadows/culture: Parks Canada, via search summary. Establishes site history: Norwegian explorer Helge Ingstad found the site in 1960; archaeologist Anne Stine Ingstad led excavations from 1961 to 1968 and identified it as Norse by comparison with Greenland and Iceland sites, dating it only broadly to around AD 1000; designated a National Historic Site of Canada in 1968 and a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1978.
